newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Li Ka-shing, a classic rags-to-riches tale.
newsitem.headline: HK's Li Ka-shing, a classic rags-to-riches tale.

text.p: In Hong Kong business circles, he's known as "superman" for his Midas touch.
He may be one of the world's richest men, but he says he wears shoes with plastic soles because they last longer.

Li Ka-shing's rise from rags to riches is a classic Hong Kong story. Born in Chaozhou city, formerly Swatow, in southern China, Li was in the tide of humanity to sweep south from impoverished China into the British colony of Hong Kong where the streets were rumoured to be paved with gold.
They were for Li. Deprived of much of an education because he needed to work merely to survive, Li, now 68, is Hong Kong's most prominent businessman.
Forbes magazine named him as one of the world's 10 richest individuals in 1995.

Li has come a long way since assembling plastic flowers to ensure rice in his bowl. He now controls a global business empire in industries ranging from property, telecommunications, oil and electricity generation, to container ports.
His flagship Cheung Kong (Holdings) Ltd and conglomerate Hutchison Whampoa Ltd, are regarded as among the bluest of Hong Kong's blue chips.
The two together represent a market capitalisation of about HK$365 billion (US$47.17 billion) out of a total market capitalisation of around HK$3.4 trillion.
Li has not let his immense wealth go to his head and he lives modestly. He can be spotted walking the streets of the Central business district, often trailed by flocks of reporters.
"My life is rather simple and I don't need much money," he said recently.

His wealth has endowed him with significant political influence. He is a member of China's Preparatory Committee responsible for hammering out details of Hong Kong's reversion to Chinese sovereignty at midnight on June 30.
He is also an adviser to Beijing on Hong Kong affairs, and a former member of a committee that drafted Hong Kong's post-colonial constitution.
Li founded Cheung Kong, which turned out plastic trinkets, at the age of just 22, before beginning to dabble in property in the late 1950s.

Cheung Kong has ridden a property boom buoyed by Li's ability to spot a bargain and predict where the next upsurge would occur. One of his coups was to buy up land along what became Hong Kong's Mass Transit Railway.

He listed Cheung Kong in 1972 and now holds about 33.43 percent. He acquired Hutchison Whampoa Ltd, a trading house and dockyard concern, in 1979, building it up into a diversified conglomerate operating in North America, Europe and Asia.
Li has been regarded as the kingpin of his business empire, but speculation is growing in Hong Kong circles that he is gradually stepping out of the business world.

Newspaper reports have quoted him as saying he would like to do "something meaningful". They say he has told friends he would like to gradually hand over more company business to his elder son, Victor.
"I hope when I grow older, I will do more medical and educational work," one report quoted Li as saying.
On Monday the group announced a major corporate reshuffle which industry analysts said appeared designed to ensure the Li family's long-term dominance of the group and simplify its structure.
Widowed in 1990, Li has two sons, both Stanford-educated.

Victor, 32, is Cheung Kong's deputy chairman and deputy managing director. He is also an executive director of Hutchison. His brother, 29-year-old Richard, is Hutchison's deputy chairman. Richard also owns Singapore-based conglomerate Pacific Century Regional Developments Ltd
